items.prompt: An ADR was accepted and written down. Does that alone guarantee the team will keep following it years later?
choices: No, someone has to keep it findable and checked
Yes, because accepted decisions bind everyone who joins later
Yes, as long as the file is in version control
No, because ADRs expire after a fixed year
items.explanation: Writing is one cheap step. Keeping the record findable, current and checked takes ongoing effort.

items.prompt: Which of these is a symptom of an ADR pile gone stale?
choices: Every ADR has exactly one named author
The ADR folder is stored in the main repository
Each ADR is shorter than one printed page
Nobody can find the ADR that governs this code
items.explanation: When nobody can locate the governing ADR, discoverability has decayed.

items.prompt: A new engineer re-argues a settled trade-off from scratch. Which decay does this show most?
choices: Compilation, the build is too slow
Latency, the review process took far too long
Discoverability, they never found the old ADR
Encryption, the record was unreadable
items.explanation: The newcomer never found the old ADR, which is a discoverability failure.

items.prompt: Two services quietly break an accepted ADR and nobody notices. Which decay is that?
choices: Discoverability, the file is hidden away somewhere
Enforcement, nothing checks the code
Legitimacy, the board refused it
Naming, the ADR title is unclear
items.explanation: The record is fine but nothing compares the code to it, which is an enforcement failure.

items.prompt: What does 'legitimacy' decay mean for a pile of ADRs?
choices: Unclear who may reopen a decision
The ADRs are copied without permission
The documents contain spelling errors
The authors have changed their job titles
items.explanation: Legitimacy decays when it is unclear who may reopen a decision or how.

items.prompt: Which is the cheapest part of ADR work at scale?
choices: Keeping a hundred ADRs trustworthy
Enforcing every ADR in the code
Knowing which ADR governs a file
Writing one new ADR
items.explanation: One ADR is easy to write and reason about. The hard part is trust across a growing pile.

items.prompt: Why does a pile of 100 ADRs behave differently from a single ADR?
choices: Larger files always load more slowly
More ADRs means each is less detailed
Nobody can tell which are still true
Git cannot store that many documents
items.explanation: With many records by people who have left, readers cannot tell which are still true.

items.prompt: An ADR's author has left the company. What risk does that add?
choices: The ADR is deleted from version control
Nobody remembers the reasoning behind it
The ADR automatically becomes deprecated
The ADR must be rewritten in a new format
items.explanation: The reasoning lived in people's heads, and once they leave, nobody can explain why the decision was made.

items.prompt: A team has 118 ADRs, 17 of them accepted but overdue for review. Which statement best explains why that number is a governance problem?
choices: Seventeen is above the legal limit for open decisions
They claim to be in force without recent review
Overdue ADRs cannot be read until they are reviewed
The pile has been counted in the wrong format entirely
items.explanation: An accepted ADR claims to govern the code. Without a recent review, nothing confirms that claim, so it is risk, not a legal matter.
items.reference:
What decays in an unmanaged pile
🔍 discoverability: nobody can find the ADR
🧱 enforcement: code drifts, nobody notices
⚖️ legitimacy: reopening is impossible or free
✍️ writing it down once fixes none of these
Why: a decision only stays alive if something tends it on purpose.
items.learnMore:
A record is not a rule

An accepted ADR is a sentence in a file. Nobody is paid to remember it, so as people leave and code changes, it becomes harder to find, easier to violate, and unclear whether it can be reopened.

Common mistake

Assuming that because a decision exists in writing, the team still follows it.
items.reflection: Think of a rule in a shared flat or club that everyone once agreed to. How would a newcomer find out about it, and who would notice when it was broken?

items.prompt: A reviewer says 'we decided against this' but cannot show the record, and the author proceeds anyway. Which cure addresses the root problem?
choices: A maintained, searchable status on every ADR
A stricter rule that reviewers must memorize ADRs
A policy that authors never question old decisions
A larger folder of design documents per service
items.explanation: A maintained status makes the live decision findable. Memorizing records or forbidding questions does not scale or survive turnover.

items.prompt: Which status means the ADR is currently in force?
choices: proposed
accepted
superseded
deprecated
items.explanation: accepted is the only status that means in force.

items.prompt: An ADR is 'proposed'. Should new code treat it as the governing decision?
choices: No, it has not been ratified
Yes, it is the newest decision
Yes, once one reviewer comments
Only on weekdays after circulation
items.explanation: proposed means not yet ratified, so it does not govern new code.

items.prompt: What does 'superseded' tell you?
choices: The ADR was never written down properly
The service it covers was shut down
The ADR needs another round of edits
A newer ADR replaced it, follow that
items.explanation: superseded means a later ADR took over, so follow the link.

items.prompt: What does 'deprecated' mean on an ADR?
choices: It was replaced by a newer ADR on record
It is waiting for the board to ratify it
It no longer applies, with no replacement
It was accepted but needs a formatting fix
items.explanation: deprecated means no longer applies, and nothing replaces it.

items.prompt: Which status carries a link to a replacement ADR?
choices: proposed
superseded
deprecated
accepted
items.explanation: Only superseded carries a pointer to the replacement.

items.prompt: Which statuses mean 'do not govern new code'? Pick the best answer.
choices: all except accepted
only the superseded status
only the deprecated status
proposed and accepted together
items.explanation: Only accepted governs. The other three are history or draft.

items.prompt: Who should decide that a proposed ADR becomes accepted?
choices: Whoever opens the pull request
The newest engineer on the team
A script that counts the comments
The review body
items.explanation: Ratification belongs to the review body so that accepted means something.

items.prompt: Why is an out-of-date status field harmful?
choices: It makes the file larger to download
It breaks the syntax of the document
It asks readers to trust a bare claim
It forces a second copy of the ADR
items.explanation: A stale status asks readers to trust a claim that nothing backs.

items.prompt: ADR-031 says 'superseded by ADR-077'. A developer reads only ADR-031 and designs to it. What went wrong?
choices: They skipped the proposal stage entirely
They used a deprecated library by accident
They followed a record that is out of date
They read a file that was never ratified
items.explanation: ADR-031 is history. The live decision is ADR-077, which the status pointed to.
items.reference:
Four statuses
📝 proposed: written, not yet ratified
✅ accepted: in force
➡️ superseded: replaced, follow the link
🗑️ deprecated: gone, nothing replaces it
Why: only accepted governs new code; superseded points you onward.
items.learnMore:
Status is a claim readers rely on

Each status answers 'should I follow this?' A superseded record is history with a pointer to the live decision. A deprecated one has no pointer because there is nothing to follow.

Common mistake

Reading the title and ignoring the status.
items.reflection: Think of a recipe card that says 'old version, see the card in the blue folder'. What would go wrong if that note were missing or wrong?

items.prompt: An old service was shut down and its ADR now describes a system that does not exist. Which status fits?
choices: superseded, because the service is gone
deprecated, because nothing replaces it
proposed, because it needs reconfirming
accepted, because it was once ratified
items.explanation: The service is gone and nothing took over its decision, which is what deprecated means.

Search for the longest document about the topic
Ask whoever wrote the most recent proposal
Follow superseded links to an accepted ADR

items.prompt: Which mechanism checks that the codebase still honors a decision?
choices: A review board for design
A status field in the file
A fitness function
A design document
items.explanation: Fitness functions check the code against a decision, usually in CI.

items.prompt: Which mechanism gives 'is this still current?' an owner?
choices: A fitness function
A board
A code formatter
A status label alone
items.explanation: A board gives reopening and confirmation an owner.

items.prompt: Where do fitness functions usually run?
choices: In CI on every pull request
Only at yearly planning meetings
Inside the ADR document itself
On the author's laptop at will
items.explanation: CI runs the checks on every pull request, so drift is caught early.

items.prompt: What does a lifecycle status tell a reader?
choices: How many people voted for it
Which language the code uses
When the next release ships
Whether it is in force
items.explanation: Status says whether a decision is in force and where to go next.

items.prompt: Does an architecture review board need to be large and formal?
choices: Yes, it needs at least twenty members
Yes, it must include every team lead
No, a small group with authority works
No, it should have no authority at all
items.explanation: A small standing group with real authority is enough.

items.prompt: A check fails the build when checkout imports ledger. Which mechanism is that?
choices: A review board
A fitness function
A status transition
A superseding ADR
items.explanation: A check that fails the build on a forbidden import is a fitness function.

items.prompt: Which mechanism keeps a superseded ADR pointing to its replacement?
choices: Lifecycle status
Fitness functions
Code formatting
Build caching
items.explanation: Status carries the pointer from an old decision to its replacement.

items.prompt: Why not rely on engineers remembering every ADR?
choices: Engineers are not allowed to read ADRs
ADRs are too short to remember
Memory is slower than a build
Memory fades and people leave
items.explanation: People forget and leave, so enforcement cannot rest on memory.

items.prompt: A team has accurate statuses and an active board, yet two services break an accepted ADR for months. Which missing mechanism explains it?
choices: A longer status vocabulary on each ADR
A second review board for sign-off
A rule that authors reread their records
A fitness function that checks the code
items.explanation: Accurate statuses and a board do not look at imports. Only a fitness function does.
items.reference:
Mechanism to problem
🏷️ lifecycle status: is it in force?
🏛️ review board: who may reopen it?
🤖 fitness function: does the code still obey?
🧩 each covers a gap the other two leave
Why: no single mechanism covers findability, legitimacy and enforcement at once.
items.learnMore:
Three mechanisms, three gaps

Status keeps records honest, the board gives reopening an owner, and fitness functions check code. Dropping one leaves its gap open even if the other two are excellent.

Common mistake

Adding a review board and assuming the code now matches the ADRs.
items.reflection: Think of a building: signage says what is allowed, an inspector decides exceptions, and a sensor sounds an alarm. What happens if you keep only one?

items.explanation: Checks only verify rules. Someone must own deciding whether a decision should stand or change.

items.prompt: From which status can an ADR become 'accepted'?
choices: superseded
deprecated
rejected
proposed
items.explanation: Only a proposed ADR can be ratified into accepted.

items.prompt: Who ratifies a proposed ADR?
choices: Whoever opens the PR
The build system
The review board
The newest hire
items.explanation: Ratification is the board's job, so accepted means reviewed.

items.prompt: Which transition is legal?
choices: superseded to accepted
accepted to superseded
deprecated to accepted
rejected to accepted
items.explanation: accepted to superseded is a legal edge. The others lead into accepted.

items.prompt: Is there a legal edge from 'superseded' back to 'accepted'?
choices: No, a revival is a new ADR
Yes, by editing the status field
Yes, if the author agrees
Yes, after thirty days pass
items.explanation: There is no such edge. Reviving a decision means a new ADR.

items.prompt: What are the end states of the machine?
choices: proposed and accepted together
accepted only, nothing else
proposed only, nothing else
rejected, superseded, deprecated
items.explanation: Rejected, superseded and deprecated have no outgoing edges.

items.prompt: What does the machine attach to every edge?
choices: A deadline in calendar days
A numeric score from one to ten
An actor allowed to cross it
A copy of the previous document
items.explanation: Each edge names who may cross it, which keeps edits controlled.

items.prompt: Which transition fits 'we abandoned the approach and nothing replaces it'?
choices: accepted to superseded
accepted to deprecated
proposed to accepted
proposed to rejected
items.explanation: An abandoned approach with no replacement ends as deprecated.

items.prompt: Why use a state machine instead of a free-text status?
choices: It blocks arbitrary edits
It makes the ADR file shorter on disk
It lets the build run faster overall
It removes the need for any reviewers
items.explanation: Controlled edges keep the status trustworthy.

items.prompt: A routine PR changes 'deprecated' to 'accepted' on ADR-020 with the message 'bringing it back'. What is the correct handling?
choices: Reject it, since a revival needs a new ADR
Approve it, since the author knows the history best
Approve it, since statuses are only labels anyway
Reject it, since deprecated records cannot be edited
items.explanation: Reviving a deprecated decision is a new decision. It needs its own ratification, not a label flip.
items.reference:
Legal transitions
📝 proposed → accepted or rejected, by the board
✅ accepted → superseded or deprecated
🚫 no edge back into accepted
🧑‍⚖️ every edge has a named actor
Why: a status is only trustworthy if changing it is controlled.
items.learnMore:
Free text versus controlled edges

A flat string can be changed by anyone to anything. A state machine names the legal edges and who may cross them, so a reader can trust the current value.

Common mistake

Letting a routine pull request flip an old status back.
items.reflection: Think of a parcel tracking page. Why would you stop trusting it if anyone could edit the status by hand?

items.prompt: ADR-050 is accepted and a new ADR-090 replaces its approach. What should ADR-050's final status be, and what should it carry?
choices: deprecated, with no link to anything
rejected, with a note from the author
proposed, with a link to ADR-090
superseded, with a link to ADR-090
items.explanation: The old ADR becomes superseded and links forward, so readers can follow the chain.

items.prompt: How should someone formally reopen ADR-042?
choices: Write a new ADR that targets it
Edit the old ADR's status by hand
Delete the old ADR from the repo
Mention it in a chat message
items.explanation: A new ADR that targets the old one makes the reopening formal.

items.prompt: What must a reopening ADR state?
choices: Who will be unhappy with the change
How many people voted last time
The exact date the code was written
What has changed since the original
items.explanation: The proposal must say what changed since the original decision.

items.prompt: What does a reopening ADR leave behind?
choices: Nothing, the debate is just talk
A deleted copy of the old decision
A searchable record
A longer meeting calendar
items.explanation: The record shows the question was reopened and answered.

items.prompt: Is reopening a decision forbidden?
choices: Yes, accepted decisions are frozen
No, it must justify itself
Yes, unless the author approves it
No, and it needs no justification
items.explanation: Reopening is allowed, but it has to justify itself on the record.

items.prompt: What problem does re-arguing in chat cause?
choices: The same debate returns, unrecorded
The chat tool runs out of storage
The ADR is converted to a new format
Reviewers lose their access rights
items.explanation: A chat leaves nothing searchable, so the same argument can return.

items.prompt: Which is a good 'what changed' reason?
choices: A newer engineer prefers the other option
The meeting ran out of time yesterday
The old document is somewhat long
The original constraint no longer holds
items.explanation: A changed constraint is a legitimate reason. A preference alone is weaker.

items.prompt: Why link the new ADR to the old one?
choices: It makes the build pass more quickly
It deletes the old decision's text
Readers can follow the chain
It gives the old author a promotion
items.explanation: Links let a reader follow the sequence from old decision to new one.

items.prompt: After a successful reopening, what happens to the old ADR?
choices: It is erased so no one can read it
It becomes superseded, with a link
It stays accepted beside the new one
It returns to proposed for another vote
items.explanation: The old ADR is superseded and points to its replacement.

items.prompt: Nothing about the constraints changed, but a lead prefers the other approach and files a new ADR. How should the 'what changed' section read?
choices: Invent a changed constraint to justify the switch
State plainly that this is a preference reversal
Leave the section empty and rely on seniority
Skip the ADR and edit the old one quietly
items.explanation: Honesty about a preference reversal is the point. It makes the case harder, which stops needless churn.
items.reference:
Two ways to reopen
💬 re-argue in chat: debate repeats, nothing recorded
📄 new ADR targeting the old one: record kept
❓ must state what changed since the original
🔎 searchable proof the question was reopened
Why: reopening is allowed, but it has to justify itself on the record.
items.learnMore:
Cost of an honest reopening

A new ADR must say what changed. If nothing did, it must admit a preference reversal, which is a harder case to win. That friction stops endless re-litigation without freezing decisions.

Common mistake

Treating 'it is allowed to reopen' as 'it is free to reopen'.
items.reflection: Think of a club that votes to change a rule. What makes a second vote fair, and what makes it just a rerun?

items.prompt: A new engineer's design doc argues against ADR-042 without mentioning it. Which response keeps the record useful?
choices: Ask for a new ADR that targets ADR-042
Block the doc because the author is new

Meeting on different days
Reviewing more ADRs monthly

Fewer reviewers
Tiering by blast radius of each ADR
Bigger agendas

items.prompt: Arrivals are 10 per month and the board reviews 4. How many unreviewed ADRs after 6 months?
items.explanation: 10 - 4 = 6 per month, and 6 x 6 = 36.
items.reference:
Backlog grows by the gap
📥 arrivals: 8 ADRs per month (assumed)
📤 reviews: 5 ADRs per month (assumed)
➕ net: +3 per month, 36 after 12 months

Why: what matters is the sign of the gap, not the raw numbers.

items.prompt: A board approves every proposal. What does that suggest?
choices: It is exceptionally efficient
It has too few members
It may be rubber-stamping
It reads proposals too carefully
items.explanation: A board that never says no is adding delay, not judgment.

items.prompt: An ADR is amended but its check is not. What is the risk?
choices: The ADR is automatically deleted
It blocks or misses the wrong things
The board stops meeting entirely
The build runs twice as long
items.explanation: A check out of step with its ADR blocks the wrong things or misses the right ones.

items.prompt: Is full ADR governance always worth it?
choices: No, tiny teams may not need it
Yes, for any team of any size
Yes, as long as there is one ADR
No, it is always a waste

choices: Write even more ADRs
Close the board down
Delete their statuses
Decide informally off the record, quietly
items.explanation: People who find the process too heavy decide off the record.

items.prompt: Which is a sign of a healthy board?
choices: It accepts everything within a day
It never meets in person
It sometimes says no
It deletes rejected proposals
items.explanation: A board that sometimes refuses is exercising judgment.

items.prompt: A five-person team has six ADRs everyone has read. Best approach?
choices: Set up a full board and CI checks now
Keep it light until it must grow
Ban further ADRs altogether
Merge all ADRs into one file
items.explanation: Light touch fits a small team until the pile outgrows memory.

items.prompt: Which action keeps a fitness function trustworthy?
choices: Updating it with its ADR
Never touching it after launch
Disabling it during releases
Letting each team rewrite it
items.explanation: Updating the check alongside the ADR keeps them aligned.

items.prompt: Why can informal off-record decisions undermine governance?
choices: They make ADR files larger
They shorten the board's meetings
They remove the need for statuses
Violations return unnoticed
items.explanation: Off-record decisions bring back the silent violations governance exists to prevent.

items.prompt: A board accepts every proposal within a day and nobody cites an ADR in design discussions. What is the best diagnosis?
choices: The board is correctly tuned for speed
The ADRs are too long to cite
The statuses are in the wrong order
The board adds latency, not judgment
items.explanation: Instant universal approval with no citations means ADRs are not shaping decisions, only delaying them.
items.reference:
Three ways governance fails
🔏 rubber-stamp board: all yes, no judgment
🧮 check drifted from its ADR: false blocks or gaps
🐢 one heavy process for everything: teams route around it
🌱 tiny team: machinery may cost more than it returns
Why: governance needs its own upkeep and its own scale test.
items.learnMore:
The machinery can rot too

A board that never refuses adds delay with no filtering. A check that no longer matches its ADR trains people to bypass checks. A uniform heavy process makes teams decide off the record.

Common mistake

Treating governance as finished once the board and checks exist.
items.reflection: Think of a security gate that always opens, or a rule list nobody updates. How do people behave around it?
